title: Perfect pitch and tonal languages
hook: Speaking a tonal language as a child may make perfect pitch far more likely.
peek: Perfect pitch, naming a note with no reference, is rare among Western musicians. Research by the psychologist Diana Deutsch found it far more common among music students who grew up speaking Mandarin, hinting that early speech trains the ear.
lede: Most people, even many fine musicians, hear notes in relation to each other. A small minority can hear a single note and name it, the way most of us name a colour. This is called absolute or perfect pitch, and it is often estimated to occur in roughly one person in 10,000 in Western countries. Where it shows up more often is the surprise.

bullets.text: In Mandarin, the syllable "ma" can mean mother, hemp, horse or scold depending on its pitch contour. Children who grow up with a tonal language learn early that pitch carries meaning.
Deutsch and colleagues compared music students in Beijing and in New York State. Among those who started lessons at the same early age, far more of the Mandarin speakers had perfect pitch.

Almost everyone with perfect pitch began musical training young, often before about age six. Researchers think the ability depends on learning during an early window, rather than being purely inherited.
Deutsch also found that when two Shepard tones are played half an octave apart, some people hear the pair rise and others hear it fall. The answer seems linked to the speech people grew up hearing.

Tonal languages can be whistled, because the tune of the words carries so much meaning, and whistled speech exists in parts of Africa, Asia and the Americas. On La Gomera, islanders whistle Spanish, which is not tonal, by mimicking its vowels and consonants.

Perfect pitch is anchored to a convention. The note A above middle C was standardised at 440 vibrations per second in the twentieth century; in earlier centuries the same A often sat noticeably lower or higher.
